title: Tennis Elbow: Do I Need a Steroid Injection, or Is Physiotherapy Enough?
metaDescription: Tennis elbow pain on the outer elbow: how long it takes to heal, why a steroid injection may not be the first choice, and what works instead.
intro: Most tennis elbow settles without surgery or injections. Rest from the painful activity, medicines, and exercises for the forearm work for the large majority. A steroid injection eases pain quickly, but in a good trial people who had it were more likely to have the pain return within a year. So we usually keep it for later.

sections.heading: What is tennis elbow?
sections.body: Pain on the outer side of the elbow from strain on the forearm tendons. You do not need to play tennis; gripping, lifting and repetitive forearm work cause it. The AAOS (OrthoInfo) says it usually affects people aged 30 to 50 and comes on gradually, with a weaker grip and sometimes pain at night.

sections.heading: Will it get better without surgery?
sections.body: Very likely. OrthoInfo says about 80 to 95 out of every 100 patients do well without surgery. Recovery takes weeks to months, so patience and a steady routine matter.

sections.heading: What is our usual order of treatment?
sections.body: We usually start simple and move up only if you are not improving.
bullets: Rest from painful activities for a few weeks and use pain relief gels or tablets.
Once the pain has eased, forearm stretching and strengthening exercises, with a brace if it helps.
If pain persists, physiotherapy treatments such as ultrasound or shockwave, for pain relief.
Injection only if still needed, for pain relief.

sections.heading: Why not an injection first?
sections.body: In a trial of 165 adults, those given a steroid injection felt better quickly, but at one year they were less likely to be fully recovered and more likely to have the pain come back than those given a dummy injection. OrthoInfo also advises using steroid injections very sparingly.

sections.heading: Are PRP and shockwave worth trying?
sections.body: The evidence is not strong. OrthoInfo says PRP studies are mixed and many doctors consider shockwave experimental. A Cochrane review found too little proof for platelet-rich treatments in tendon injuries. They may help some people with pain, but they should not replace exercises. We use them for pain relief only.

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body: Only if you have had no improvement after 6 to 12 months of proper treatment. OrthoInfo reports good results in 80 to 90 out of 100 people, though some strength loss is not unusual. Most people never need it.

faqs.q: How long does tennis elbow take to heal?
faqs.a: Usually several weeks to months. Most improve without surgery.

faqs.q: Is a cortisone shot good for tennis elbow?
faqs.a: It relieves pain quickly but may make the pain more likely to return later. OrthoInfo advises caution.

faqs.q: Should I wear a tennis elbow brace?
faqs.a: A brace over the forearm can ease symptoms for some people while the tendon rests.

faqs.q: Can I keep working with tennis elbow?
faqs.a: Often yes, with changes to how you grip and lift. We can advise for your job.

faqs.q: What is the difference between tennis elbow and golfer's elbow?
faqs.a: Tennis elbow hurts on the outer side of the elbow; golfer's elbow on the inner side.
